name: Highland Puebla Nahuatl
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Highland Puebla Nahuatl (high1278, azz) is not in the catalog. The sweep had one title-keyword item, Robinson 1969 'Puebla (Sierra) Nahuat prosodies' (SIL Publications in Linguistics 22, pp. 15-32), which was already fetched sources (Wayback copy of the sil.org PDF, scanned, scanned) under by an earlier pass; I re-read the scanned and verified the deciding passage against the page image. It is a first-hand phonology of the Zacapoaxtla (Xalacapan) dialect and states that word-level accent (stress plus raised pitch) is penultimate in polysyllables, retained under compounding, with antepenultimate accent when one of four post-clitics (-ti, -sah, -ok, -ya) is suffixed and pre-antepenultimate when two are stacked; monosyllabic free morphemes are stressed, bound monosyllables are not (sec. 3.2 p. 19; fn. 26 p. 32). Vowel length is independent of stress. The same author's Aztec Studies II (1970, p. 1-2, on file) summarizes 'primary stress is on the penultimate syllable of the word - except for a few patterns of ultimate and antepenultimate placement', and fn. 3 quotes McQuown 1942 on the Nauzontla variety (mostly penultimate, a good number antepenultimate, a few final). This is a suitable deciding source for a new catalog record: penultimate, quantity-insensitive, clitic-extrametrical. Not obtained (already noted): Key & Key 1953 IJAL 19:53-56 (paywalled, DOI page returned 403), Key & Ritchie de Key 1953 vocabulary (sil.org Cloudflare-blocked), Robinson 1966 Hartford dissertation (archive.org lending-restricted), McQuown 1942, Troiani 1979 -- none is expected to outrank Robinson 1969, so acquisition priority is low. updated with a dated sweep line.

earlier_scan.source_named: Key, Harold & Mary R. Key. 1953. The phonemes of Sierra Nahuat. IJAL 19:53-56 (Zacapoaxtla = Highland Puebla Nahuatl). JSTOR-paywalled; Wikipedia phonology summary omits stress.

new_statements.quote: 3.2 There are four emic micro-segments, based on the contrastive placement of accent. (1) Monosyllabic micro-segments have an accent: "taal 'earth', "aat 'water', "et 'beans', "ca 'with'. (2) Most polysyllabic micro-segments receive penultimate accent: "taagat 'man', "yoliik 'he was born', na"nakat 'mushroom', či"kawak 'he's strong', čiči"pika 'it drips'. The basic accent pattern of micro-segments is retained in the compounding processes. (3) An antepenultimate accent pattern occurs when any of the following syllables (post-clitics) is suffixed to a polysyllabic micro-segment: -ti 'nominalizer', -sah 'just', -ok 'still', -ya 'now'. ... an antepenultimate accent pattern: "tepos 'metal', "teposti 'metal', "tepossah 'just metal'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word (micro-segment) accent = stress plus raised pitch, predictable: monosyllables are accented; polysyllabic words are accented on the penult. The post-clitics -ti (nominalizer/absolutive), -sah 'just', -ok 'still', -ya 'now' do not shift the accent, so forms with one such clitic surface with antepenultimate accent and with two clitics pre-antepenultimate (tépos, téposti, tépostisah); all other suffixation re-places accent on the new penult. Any morpheme of two or more syllables has penultimate stress, retained (as tertiary) in compounds.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Three degrees of accent by prosodic domain: primary accent on the nucleus of the macro-segment (clause), secondary accent + high pitch on the nucleus (final micro-segment, penultimate syllable) of the meso-segment (phonological phrase ~ grammatical word), tertiary accent on the penult of non-final micro-segments (roots) inside compounds/phrases. Free monosyllabic morphemes bear stress; bound monosyllables do not (fn. 26).
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate (and pre-antepenultimate) accent with the enclitics -ti, -sah, -ok, -ya (one or two stacked); a small set of high-pitched particles (nohón 'that', aačáa 'perhaps', akcáa 'someone') whose pitch is unaffected by stress; Robinson 1970 also mentions 'a few patterns of ultimate... placement'. McQuown 1942 (Nauzontla, quoted fn. 3) likewise reports mostly penultimate with a good number of antepenultimate and a few final-stressed forms.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain of the basic rule is the micro-segment (phonological word, 1-6 syllables, never in isolation); the grammatical word with ordinary suffixes = meso-segment, whose nucleus keeps penultimate secondary accent; examples are from texts, conversation and paradigms gathered around Zacapoaxtla (Xalacapan).
new_statements.identity_note: Robinson 1969/1970 describe 'Sierra Nahuat' (SN) from Xalacapan, municipio of Zacapoaxtla, Puebla (fieldwork 1958-62); fn. 5 defines the dialect as the area bounded by Teziutlan, Zautla, Tetela de Ocampo and Cuetzalan with Zacapoaxtla at its centre = Glottolog high1278 / ISO azz (Highland Puebla / Sierra Puebla Nahuatl). Key & Key 1953 describe the same Zacapoaxtla variety. McQuown 1942 (quoted second-hand) is Nauzontla, same dialect area; Troiani 1979 is San Miguel Tzinacapan (Cuetzalan), also within azz.

new_statements.quote: 3.2 There are four emic micro-segments, based on the contrastive placement of accent. (1) Monosyllabic micro-segments have an accent: "taal 'earth', "aat 'water', "et 'beans', "ca 'with'. (2) Most polysyllabic micro-segments receive penultimate accent: "taagat 'man', "yoliik 'he was born', na"nakat 'mushroom', či"kawak 'he's strong', čiči"pika 'it drips'. The basic accent pattern of micro-segments is retained in the compounding processes. (3) An antepenultimate accent pattern occurs when any of the following syllables (post-clitics) is suffixed to a polysyllabic micro-segment: -ti 'nominalizer', -sah 'just', -ok 'still', -ya 'now'. [fn. 26:] In grammatical terms, any morpheme of two or more syllables has penultimate stress and that stress will be retained in compounding. A free morpheme of one syllable has stress. Bound morphemes of one syllable do not have stress.

new_statements.reading: Fixed penultimate word stress (stress-cum-high-pitch on the penult of the stem/word), quantity-insensitive (long vowels do not attract stress), with morphologically conditioned antepenultimate and pre-antepenultimate stress when the extrametrical post-clitics -ti, -sah, -ok, -ya are added (one clitic -> antepenult, two -> pre-antepenult); monosyllabic free words stressed. Coding candidate: penultimate, fixed/morphological, clitic-extrametrical; not weight-sensitive.

sources.note: Sec. 1.1, pp. 1-2: 'There are three emic stresses: primary, secondary, and weak. Placement of primary stress is on the penultimate syllable of the word - except for a few patterns of ultimate and antepenultimate placement. Only non-penultimate stress is marked in Nahuat word examples in this grammar. A word is defined phonologically as ending with the syllable which follows the primary stress.'
